summary: Defines a profile of OCSP for large-scale PKI environments and for those needing a light solution, reducing bandwidth and client processing. It was replaced by RFC 9919.

plainLanguage.summary: A lighter way to ask whether a digital ID has been canceled when millions of people ask. A newer RFC replaced this.

questions: why use http get for ocsp
subtitle: A trimmed-down way to run OCSP so that millions of certificate checks can be cached and answered cheaply.

tldr.problem: OCSP was designed for real-time answers to each request, which does not scale to PKIs with millions of certificates or to mobile clients with little bandwidth and processing power.
tldr.mechanism: The profile restricts what OCSP requests and responses may contain, asks for responses to be pre-produced with clear validity times, and defines HTTP GET and caching rules so responses can be cached in the network and on the client.
tldr.outcome: It has been obsoleted by RFC 9919 and updated by RFC 8996, so current deployments should look at the newer document.

today: RFC 5019 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9919 and updated by RFC 8996. Use the newer RFC for the current specification.

sections.title: Why a Lightweight OCSP Profile
sections.content:
The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP, RFC 2560) checks whether a certificate has been revoked, as an alternative to Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs). Early deployments protected high-value transactions such as banking, so responders generated a fresh answer for every request.

That model does not scale to PKIs where millions or hundreds of millions of certificates are issued, or to mobile environments where bandwidth is at a premium and clients are constrained. This profile aims to permit three things: pre-production and distribution of OCSP responses, smaller messages, and caching of responses both in the network and on the client.

OCSP cannot signal responder capabilities, so clients need an out-of-band way to know a responder follows this profile. Where none exists, a fully conformant RFC 2560 client still interoperates with a responder operating as this profile describes.
sections.plainLanguage: If a whole town keeps asking the same question, it is better to write the answer on a poster than to answer each person one by one.

sections.title: The Profiled Requests and Responses
sections.content:
A request MUST contain only one Request in its request list, and clients MUST use SHA1 for the issuerNameHash and issuerKeyHash values. Clients MUST NOT include singleRequestExtensions and SHOULD NOT include requestExtensions; if they do, only the nonce extension is recommended. Clients SHOULD NOT send signed requests, and responders MAY ignore the signature.

Responders MUST generate a BasicOCSPResponse. A response SHOULD hold only one SingleResponse, though more are allowed to help pre-generation or caching, and SHOULD NOT include responseExtensions. Clients MUST validate the response signature. If a delegate of the CA signed it, its certificate MUST be referenced in BasicOCSPResponse.certs, and the profile recommends the id-pkix-ocsp-nocheck extension on that short-lived certificate. Responders SHOULD identify themselves with byKey to save bytes.

A responder without authoritative records for a certificate MUST return the status unauthorized. This includes responders that pre-produce responses and so cannot sign a 'successful' but 'unknown' answer.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say to keep each question and answer short and plain, about one certificate at a time, so they are cheap to send and easy to copy.

sections.title: Timestamps and Freshness
sections.content:
When responses are pre-produced, thisUpdate is the time the status is known to be correct, nextUpdate is the time at or before which newer information will be available, and producedAt is the time the response was signed. Responders MUST always include nextUpdate to help caching. Times MUST be GMT in the form YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ, including seconds and with no fractional seconds.

A client has two ways to know a response is fresh: a nonce or the clock. Because nonces are optional here, clients MUST be able to judge freshness by time. The current time must fall between thisUpdate and nextUpdate; a response with no nextUpdate, or one already past it, MUST be rejected. A client MAY allow a small tolerance for clock differences. A client that sent a nonce SHOULD NOT reject a response only because the nonce is missing, and a client that sent none MUST ignore any nonce in the reply.

On discovery, clients MUST support the authorityInfoAccess extension and the id-ad-ocsp method. If a certificate also lists a CRL, the client SHOULD try the OCSP responder first. Applications MUST verify signatures on signed data and certificate chains before requesting an OCSP check, and clients SHOULD NOT check expired certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each answer has a 'good from' time and a 'good until' time, like the dates on milk. If the answer is past its date, you throw it out and ask again.

sections.title: HTTP Transport and Caching
sections.content:
Responders MUST support OCSP over HTTP. If a request is 255 bytes or less in total, clients MUST use GET so the response can be cached; larger requests SHOULD use POST. For GET, the client base64-encodes the request, URL-encodes it, and appends it to the URI from the AIA extension, with no CR or LF characters.

Responses that can be cached carry HTTP headers: last-modified (the thisUpdate time), expires (the nextUpdate time), an ETag (recommended to be the hex SHA1 hash of the response), and cache-control with max-age, public, no-transform and must-revalidate. Responders MUST NOT put no-cache or no-store in authoritative responses.

Clients MUST cache authoritative responses locally. A responder MAY use max-age to spread out refreshes and avoid load spikes when many clients' cached copies expire together. The profile also recommends that TLS clients and servers implement the certificate status request extension, so the server can include the OCSP response in the handshake. That lowers the number of hits on the responder and reduces round trips.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the question fits in a web address, shops along the way can keep a copy of the answer and hand it out, so the main office is not bothered every time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Optional nonces open the door to replay: an old 'good' response could be shown after a certificate was revoked. The defence is an accurate clock and strict freshness checking. A client with a bad clock may reject fresh answers or accept expired ones.

Clients must validate the signature on the response and on the signer's certificate to resist man-in-the-middle and impersonation attacks. Because requests are unsigned, anyone can query a responder, which makes denial-of-service floods easier; the RFC suggests rate limiting by IP address as one measure.

HTTP headers are not cryptographically protected and may be tampered with. Clients SHOULD use them only as caching guidance, rely on the signed response, and not use a cached response beyond nextUpdate.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed, dated answer is hard to fake, but the sticky notes on the envelope are not protected, so trust the signed paper inside.

viz.caption: HEADERS ON A CACHABLE OCSP RESPONSE (RFC 5019)

data.title: Response headers
data.code:
content-type: application/ocsp-response
content-length: <OCSP response length>
last-modified: <producedAt [HTTP] date>
ETag: "<strong validator>"
expires: <nextUpdate [HTTP] date>
cache-control: max-age=<n>, public, no-transform, must-revalidate
date: <current [HTTP] date>
